Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $X$ and $Y$ be real Hilbert spaces and let $K:X\to Y$ be a compact linear operator of infinite rank, viewed as an inverse model with exact datum $Kx$. Here compact means that the image of every bounded subset has compact closure. Write $N(K)=\{x\in X:Kx=0\}$ and $H_0=\overline{\operatorname{ran}K}$. Fix a positive singular system $(s_j,v_j,u_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$ for $K$, where $\mathbb N=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$, $s_1\ge s_2\ge\cdots>0$, $s_j\to0$, $Kv_j=s_ju_j$, $(v_j)$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $N(K)^\perp$, and $(u_j)$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $H_0$. A complete orthonormal basis is an orthonormal family whose closed linear span is the whole indicated subspace. These are the compact SVD conventions; in particular, this model concerns minimum-norm representatives in $N(K)^\perp$ and does not estimate a kernel component.

For a truth $x\in N(K)^\perp$, let $\theta_j=\langle x,v_j\rangle_X$. The complete-basis coefficient map identifies $N(K)^\perp$ bijectively and isometrically with $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$, so every $\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ is a model parameter. For $\epsilon>0$, take the functional white-noise experiment on the separable Hilbert space $H_0$ with observations $Y_x(g)=\langle Kx,g\rangle_Y+\epsilon W(g)$, where $W$ is centered, has covariance $\mathbb E[W(g)W(h)]=\langle g,h\rangle_Y$, and has independent standard-normal values on every finite orthonormal tuple. The countable complete basis makes $H_0$ separable. Define $\xi_j=W(u_j)$ and $Z_j=Y_x(u_j)/s_j$. The sequence sample space is $\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$ with the product Borel sigma-algebra, meaning the sigma-algebra generated by its coordinate projections. The coordinate law is the pushforward of the functional experiment under $y\mapsto(y(u_j)/s_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$; this map is measurable because each coordinate is a cylinder evaluation followed by scalar multiplication. The compact SVD expansion gives $\langle Kx,u_j\rangle_Y=s_j\theta_j$, and the positive-noise white-noise coordinate theorem gives the independent standard-normal coordinates $\xi_j$. Hence the normalized coordinates satisfy $Z_j=\theta_j+\epsilon s_j^{-1}\xi_j,\qquad j\in\mathbb N.$

For the zero-noise boundary $\epsilon=0$, define the sequence experiment separately by the point mass at $\theta$, so $Z_j=\theta_j$. This boundary is not an instance of the positive-noise functional experiment.

An **experiment** is a measurable space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, a set $\Theta$ of
parameter labels, and a family $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ of probability
measures on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ ([[def-measurable-space]],
[[def-probability-measure]]). The measures $P_\theta$ are the sampling laws.
If data under a parameter value are realized as a random element, its law is
the pushforward measure $P_X(B)=P(X^{-1}(B))$ from
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]; it is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]].

The definition specifies the family of laws only. It supplies no sigma-algebra
on $\Theta$, no measurability condition on $\theta\mapsto P_\theta$, and no
common underlying probability space on which all observations must be realized.

A **measurable space** is a pair $(X,\mathcal A)$ consisting of a set $X$ and a
sigma-algebra $\mathcal A$ on $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]). The members of
$\mathcal A$ are the **measurable subsets** of $X$.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

Fix $n \ge 1$ and let $\lambda_n^*$ be the Lebesgue outer set function on $\mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-lebesgue-outer-measure]]). A set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is
**Lebesgue measurable** when

$$\lambda_n^*(A) \;=\; \lambda_n^*(A \cap E) \;+\; \lambda_n^*(A \setminus E) \qquad \text{for every } A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n .$$

This formula makes sense before any outer-measure theorem is invoked. Under
countable choice, [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-is-an-outer-measure-agreeing-with-volume]]
makes $\lambda_n^*$ an outer measure, and the displayed condition is then exactly
Carathéodory measurability in the sense of [[def-caratheodory-measurable-set]].

The family of Lebesgue measurable sets is written $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$,
and **Lebesgue measure** is the restriction

$$\lambda_n \;:=\; \lambda_n^*\!\restriction_{\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)} .$$

On the real line the subscript is dropped and $\lambda := \lambda_1$.

The quantifier over every test set $A$ is part of the condition, and no
hypothesis on $E$ is imposed before it is tested. That
$\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra and that $\lambda_n$ is a complete
measure on it are not part of this definition: they are proved, under the Axiom
of Countable Choice, in [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]], which is
recorded in this item's `justified_by` because it is a statement about the
objects introduced here. Until that theorem the symbols $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$
and $\lambda_n$ name a family of sets and a restricted set function, nothing more.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]), let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a measurable action space, meaning a set with
a specified sigma-algebra ([[def-measurable-space]]), and let
$L:\Theta\times\mathsf D\to[0,+\infty]$ be a loss function whose section
$a\mapsto L(\theta,a)$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable for each $\theta$. A
randomized decision rule is a probability kernel $\delta$ from the data space
to the action space ([[def-randomized-procedure-as-a-markov-kernel]]). Its
**risk** at $\theta$ is the extended nonnegative number
$$R(\theta,\delta)=\int_{\mathcal X}\left(\int_{\mathsf D}L(\theta,a)\,\delta(x,da)\right)P_\theta(dx).$$
The inner integral is a measurable function of $x$, by
[[lem-procedure-action-law-is-measurable]], so the outer nonnegative integral
is defined by [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]].
A deterministic measurable rule is included by taking its point-mass action
kernel. No measurability on $\Theta$ is required for this definition.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]) and let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a measurable **action space**: a set of available
actions equipped with a sigma-algebra of action events, hence a measurable
space ([[def-measurable-space]]). A **randomized procedure** (or
randomized decision rule) is a probability kernel $K$ from
$(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ to $(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$, in the pointwise sense
of [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. Thus $K(x,\cdot)$ is a
probability measure on $(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ for every $x\in\mathcal X$,
and $x\mapsto K(x,B)$ is $\mathcal A$-measurable for every $B\in\mathcal G$.
After observing $x$, the procedure assigns probability $K(x,B)$ to taking an
action in $B$. The kernel is specified without reference to the unknown
parameter. This definition imposes no measurable structure on $\Theta$. The
kernel is the specification of the procedure; no representation by a separate
random seed is asserted for arbitrary measurable action spaces.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be measurable
parameter and data spaces, with $\Theta$ nonempty, and let
$K:\Theta\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]$ be a probability kernel, writing
$P_\theta=K(\theta,\cdot)$ for the sampling law
([[def-parameter-measurable-statistical-model-as-markov-kernel]]). Let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a nonempty measurable action space
([[def-measurable-space]]). Let $L:\Theta\times\mathsf D\to\overline{\mathbb R}$
be measurable from the product measurable space with sigma-algebra
$\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal G$ to the extended real line with its Borel
sigma-algebra, and assume $L(\theta,a)\geq0$ for all $(\theta,a)$
([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]],
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]], [[def-extended-reals]],
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra-on-the-extended-real-line]]). A **prior** $\pi$ is a
probability measure on $\Theta$. The risk function $\theta\mapsto R(\theta,\delta)$ is measurable
under these hypotheses by kernel integration
([[def-parameter-measurable-statistical-model-as-markov-kernel]],
[[thm-measurability-of-integration-against-a-kernel]]). The **Bayes risk** of
$\delta$ under $\pi$ is
$$r_\pi(\delta)=\int_\Theta R(\theta,\delta)\,\pi(d\theta)\in[0,+\infty].$$
Its **worst-case risk** is
$$R^*(\delta)=\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}R(\theta,\delta)\in[0,+\infty],$$
and the **minimax value** is
$$V_{\rm mm}=\inf\{R^*(\delta):\delta\text{ is a measurable randomized rule from data to actions}\}\in[0,+\infty].$$
These suprema and infima are taken in the extended order on $\overline{\mathbb R}$
([[def-extended-reals]]); they exist by
[[lem-extended-reals-complete]]. The parameter set is nonempty and the rule
class is nonempty under the action-space hypothesis, so these are suprema and
infima of nonempty sets of nonnegative extended risks.
A rule is minimax if its worst-case risk equals this infimum. These definitions
make no assertion that a minimizer exists. Nonemptiness of $\mathsf D$ ensures
the rule class is nonempty: fixing any $a_0\in\mathsf D$ gives the constant
point-mass rule $x\mapsto\delta_{a_0}$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\sinh x:=\frac{\exp x-\exp(-x)}2,\qquad\cosh x:=\frac{\exp x+\exp(-x)}2,$$
$$\tanh x:=\frac{\sinh x}{\cosh x},\qquad\operatorname{sech}x:=\frac1{\cosh x}.$$
For $x\ne0$, define
$$\coth x:=\frac{\cosh x}{\sinh x},\qquad\operatorname{csch}x:=\frac1{\sinh x}.$$

The positivity of $\exp$ makes $\cosh x>0$ for every $x$. If $x\ne0$, then
$x\ne-x$, so strict increase of $\exp$ makes $\exp x\ne\exp(-x)$; hence
$\sinh x\ne0$. Thus all four quotients above are defined on exactly their
stated domains ([[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]],
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]]).

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sinh(x+y)=\sinh x\cosh y+\cosh x\sinh y,\qquad\cosh(x+y)=\cosh x\cosh y+\sinh x\sinh y,$$
$$\cosh^2x-\sinh^2x=1,\qquad(\sinh x)'=\cosh x,\qquad(\cosh x)'=\sinh x.$$
Moreover $\sinh:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is odd, strictly increasing, and onto;
$\cosh:\mathbb R\to[1,\infty)$ is even and positive, and its restriction
to $[0,\infty)$ is strictly increasing and onto $[1,\infty)$; and
$\tanh:\mathbb R\to(-1,1)$ is strictly increasing and onto. On their declared domains,
$$(\tanh x)'=\operatorname{sech}^2x,\quad(\coth x)'=-\operatorname{csch}^2x,\quad(\operatorname{sech}x)'=-\operatorname{sech}x\tanh x,\quad(\operatorname{csch}x)'=-\operatorname{csch}x\coth x.$$

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2}\,dx=\sqrt\pi.$$

Let $c < d$ be reals and let $\varphi : [c,d] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable
at every point of $[c,d]$ as a function on $[c,d]$ ([[def-derivative]]), with
$\varphi'$ integrable on $[c,d]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex with at least two elements
([[def-interval]]) with $\varphi[\,[c,d]\,] \subseteq J$, and let $f : J \to
\mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $J$ ([[def-continuity-real]]).

Then $(f\circ\varphi)\,\varphi'$ is integrable on $[c,d]$ and

$$\int_{\varphi(c)}^{\varphi(d)} f \;=\; \int_c^d (f\circ\varphi)\,\varphi' ,$$

the left-hand integral being the oriented one of [[def-oriented-integral]].

**Neither injectivity nor monotonicity of $\varphi$ is assumed**, and that is
exactly why the left-hand side is written with oriented limits: $\varphi(d)$ may
lie below $\varphi(c)$, and $\varphi$ may return to the same value many times.
The proof runs through a primitive of $f$ and the chain rule, and no inverse
function is ever formed.

**Continuity of $f$ is a hypothesis and cannot be weakened to integrability.**
With $f$ merely integrable the composite $f \circ \varphi$ need not be
integrable at all, so the right-hand side need not exist; that is
the false statement that weakens it on the companion page.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

derivations.claim: The density in the Statement is positive and continuous. The substitution $y=\theta+\sqrt{2}\tau x$ on symmetric finite intervals and [F8] show that its integral is $(\tau\sqrt{2\pi})^{-1}\sqrt{2}\tau\sqrt{\pi}=1$, so by [F2]–[F3] it defines the scalar sampling probability on the stated Borel sample space.

Write $b=\min\{r,\tau\}$ and $u=b/\tau\in[0,1]$. This location family is the scalar Gaussian coordinate experiment described in [F1]. Under the two-point prior, the likelihood ratio at observation $y$ is $p_{b,\tau}(y)/p_{-b,\tau}(y)=\exp(2by/\tau^2)$. Hence the posterior mean is $b\tanh(by/\tau^2)$ and the posterior variance is $b^2\operatorname{sech}^2(by/\tau^2)$; for any action $a$, its conditional squared loss is the square of its distance from this posterior mean plus that posterior variance. Averaging this identity over any action kernel from [F4] leaves the posterior variance as a lower bound, including the degenerate case $b=0$.

Define $I(u):=\int_{\mathbb R}\phi(x)\operatorname{sech}(ux)\,dx$. Since $\cosh t\ge1$, the integrand lies between $0$ and $\phi(x)$, whose integral is $1$ by [F8] and the affine substitution [F9]; hence $I(u)$ is finite. Since $\cosh$ is even and increasing on $[0,\infty)$ by [F6], $\operatorname{sech}(ux)\ge\operatorname{sech}(x)$ for every real $x$ and $0\le u\le1$. Therefore $I(u)\ge I(1)$, while $e^{-u^2/2}\ge e^{-1/2}$.

For $x\ge0$, [F6] gives $0\le\tanh x$ and $(\tanh x)'\le1$ because $\cosh x\ge1$; with $\tanh0=0$, [F10] yields $\tanh x\le x$. Set $g(x)=e^{-x^2/2}\cosh x$. Differentiation using [F6] and [F10] gives $g'(x)=g(x)(\tanh x-x)\le0$, so [F10] implies $g(x)\le g(0)=1$. Evenness extends $\cosh x\le e^{x^2/2}$ to all real $x$. Consequently $\phi(x)\operatorname{sech}x\ge(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2}$, and [F8] gives $I(1)\ge1/\sqrt2$.

The prior predictive density, after $x=y/\tau$, is $\tau^{-1}\phi(x)e^{-u^2/2}\cosh(ux)$, where $\phi(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}$. Multiplying by the posterior variance from step 1.2 and changing variables gives Bayes risk $B(r,\tau)=b^2e^{-u^2/2}I(u)$, with $I$ defined in step 1.3.

Steps 2.1, 1.3 and 1.4 give $B(r,\tau)\ge b^2e^{-1/2}/\sqrt2=b^2/\sqrt{2e}=T(r,\tau)/\sqrt{2e}$, where $e=\exp(1)$ by [F7]. Since the prior is supported in $[-r,r]$, the supremum risk of every rule is at least its prior-averaged risk; taking the infimum over rules and using [F4] yields $M(r,\tau)\ge B(r,\tau)$.

The constant estimator $0$ has maximum risk $r^2$, while the identity estimator $y\mapsto y$ has risk $\tau^2$ at every parameter; hence their better maximum risk is $T(r,\tau)=b^2$. This proves the projection-risk claim together with step 3.1.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $X$ and $Y$ be real Hilbert spaces and let $K:X\to Y$ be a compact linear operator of infinite rank, viewed as an inverse model with exact datum $Kx$. Here compact means that the image of every bounded subset has compact closure. Write $N(K)=\{x\in X:Kx=0\}$ and $H_0=\overline{\operatorname{ran}K}$. A complete orthonormal basis is an orthonormal family whose closed linear span is the whole indicated subspace. These are the compact SVD conventions; in particular, this model concerns minimum-norm representatives in $N(K)^\perp$ and does not estimate a kernel component.

For a truth $x\in N(K)^\perp$, let $\theta_j=\langle x,v_j\rangle_X$. The complete-basis coefficient map identifies $N(K)^\perp$ bijectively and isometrically with $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$, so every $\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ is a model parameter. The countable complete basis makes $H_0$ separable. Define $\xi_j=W(u_j)$ and $Z_j=Y_x(u_j)/s_j$. The coordinate law is the pushforward of the functional experiment under $y\mapsto(y(u_j)/s_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$; this map is measurable because each coordinate is a cylinder evaluation followed by scalar multiplication. The compact SVD expansion gives $\langle Kx,u_j\rangle_Y=s_j\theta_j$, and the positive-noise white-noise coordinate theorem gives the independent standard-normal coordinates $\xi_j$. Hence the normalized coordinates satisfy $Z_j=\theta_j+\epsilon s_j^{-1}\xi_j,\qquad j\in\mathbb N.$

For the zero-noise boundary $\epsilon=0$, define the sequence experiment separately by the point mass at $\theta$, so $Z_j=\theta_j$. This boundary is not an instance of the positive-noise functional experiment.

Let $Q\in[0,\infty)$ and let $a=(a_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$ be a nondecreasing sequence of positive real numbers, so $0<a_1\le a_2\le\cdots$. The statistical ellipsoid of radius $Q$ and weights $a$ in the Gaussian sequence inverse model is
$$\Theta_a(Q)=\left\{\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R):\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}a_j^2\theta_j^2\le Q^2\right\}.$$
No assumption that $a_j\to\infty$ is included. In particular, this definition does not assert that the ellipsoid is compact in $\ell^2$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and
$K$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces ([[def-hilbert-space]]), let
$T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a compact operator
([[def-compact-linear-operator]]), let $|T|$ and the singular values $s_n(T)$ be
as in the absolute-value definition
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]). Let
$J=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$ when $\operatorname{ran}T$ is infinite-dimensional. When
$\operatorname{ran}T$ is finite-dimensional, put
$r:=\dim\operatorname{ran}T\in\mathbb N$ ([[def-dimension]]) and let
$J=\{1,\dots,r\}$, interpreted as $\varnothing$ when $r=0$. Thus $J$ indexes
exactly the positive singular values counted with multiplicity, which we write
as $(s_j)_{j\in J}$ in nonincreasing order. Then:

1. there are orthonormal families $(e_j)_{j\in J}$ in $(\ker T)^\perp$ and
   $(f_j)_{j\in J}$ in $\overline{\operatorname{ran}T}$, indexed by exactly $J$,
   with $|T|e_j=s_je_j$ and $f_j=s_j^{-1}Te_j$ for every $j\in J$;
2. for every $x\in H$ the series converges in norm and
   $$Tx=\sum_{j\in J}s_j\langle x,e_j\rangle f_j,$$
   and its finite partial sums
   $T_n:=\sum_{j\le n}s_j\langle\cdot,e_j\rangle f_j$ satisfy
   $\|T-T_n\|\le s_{n+1}$ for every $n$ with $n+1\in J$ (and $T_n=T$ for
   $n\ge r$ when $r<+\infty$);
3. the linear map $U$ defined on the span of $\{e_j:j\in J\}$ by $Ue_j:=f_j$,
   extended by continuity to $(\ker T)^\perp$ and by zero on $\ker T$, is a
   **partial isometry** with
   $$T=U|T|,\qquad U^*U=P_{(\ker T)^\perp},\qquad U^*U\text{ is the orthogonal projection onto }(\ker T)^\perp,$$
   and $UU^*$ the orthogonal projection onto $\overline{\operatorname{ran}T}$;
4. the zero-padded sequence $(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$ is *not* used to index the
   orthonormal systems: the systems carry exactly the index set $J$ of the
   positive singular values, and the terms $s_n(T)=0$ beyond the rank in the
   finite-rank case are numerical padding only.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $X,Y$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces and let
$A:X\to Y$ be compact and bounded. Put $S=A^*A$. By
[[lem-compact-gram-operator-is-positive-and-has-kernel]], $S$ is compact,
positive, and self-adjoint, with $\ker S=\ker A$. Let $\Sigma$ be the set of
nonzero eigenvalues of $S$ and $P_t$ the orthogonal projection onto the
eigenspace of $t\in\Sigma$; let $P_0$ be the orthogonal projection onto
$\ker S$. The compact spectral multiplier of a bounded scalar function
$q:\{0\}\cup\Sigma\to\mathbb F$ is
$$q(S)x:=q(0)P_0x+\sum_{t\in\Sigma}q(t)P_tx,$$
where the finite-subset net converges in norm by
[[lem-compact-spectral-multiplier-is-well-defined]]. For $\nu>0$, define
$S^\nu$ by the multiplier $q_\nu(0)=0$ and $q_\nu(t)=t^\nu$ for $t>0$.
This multiplier is bounded: if $t\in\Sigma$ and $u\in E_t$ is a unit vector,
then $0<t=\|Su\|\le\|S\|$, so $|q_\nu(t)|\le\|S\|^\nu$.

For $\lambda>0$, the Tikhonov filter and residual filter are
$$g_\lambda(t)=\frac1{t+\lambda},\qquad r_\lambda(t)=1-tg_\lambda(t)=\frac{\lambda}{t+\lambda}.$$
The Tikhonov solution for data $y_\delta\in Y$ is
$$x_\lambda^\delta=g_\lambda(S)A^*y_\delta =(A^*A+\lambda I_X)^{-1}A^*y_\delta.$$
Indeed, the spectral decomposition gives $S+\lambda I_X$ the multiplier
$t+\lambda$ on each $E_t$ and $\lambda$ on $\ker S$, so $g_\lambda(S)$ is
its inverse, whose existence is also supplied by
[[lem-hilbert-tikhonov-normal-operator-invertible]].
The source condition of order $\nu>0$ and radius $R\ge0$ means that
$x^\dagger=S^\nu w$ for some $w\in X$ with $\|w\|\le R$. A family of
filters $g_\alpha$ with residual filters $r_\alpha(t)=1-tg_\alpha(t)$ has
qualification at least $p>0$ when, for each $0<\nu\le p$, some finite
constant $C_\nu\ge0$ satisfies
$$t^\nu|r_\alpha(t)|\le C_\nu\alpha^\nu \quad\text{for every }\alpha>0\text{ and }t\in\Sigma.$$
When $\Sigma=\varnothing$, this condition is vacuous.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $K:X\to Y$ be compact between real or complex Hilbert spaces over the same scalar field, let $\psi$ be a bounded nonnegative spectral index with $\psi(0)=0$, and let $x=\psi(|K|)w$ for some $w\in X$. Then $x\in N(K)^\perp$; consequently, among all $z\in X$ satisfying $Kz=Kx$, $x$ is the unique vector of minimum norm.

For $a>0$ and $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$a^x:=\exp(x\log a).$$
For the supplementary zero-base convention, define $0^x:=0$ when $x>0$.

The expressions $0^0$ and $0^x$ for $x<0$ are left undefined. Negative bases are not assigned arbitrary real powers.

For $a,b>0$ and $r,s\in\mathbb R$,
$$a^{r+s}=a^ra^s,\qquad (ab)^r=a^rb^r,\qquad (a/b)^r=a^r/b^r,\qquad (a^r)^s=a^{rs}.$$

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and
$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $X$ and $Y$ be real Hilbert spaces and let $K:X\to Y$ be a compact linear operator of infinite rank, viewed as an inverse model with exact datum $Kx$. Here compact means that the image of every bounded subset has compact closure. Write $N(K)=\{x\in X:Kx=0\}$ and $H_0=\overline{\operatorname{ran}K}$. Fix a positive singular system $(s_j,v_j,u_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$ for $K$, where $\mathbb N=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$, $s_1\ge s_2\ge\cdots>0$, $s_j\to0$, $Kv_j=s_ju_j$, $(v_j)$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $N(K)^\perp$, and $(u_j)$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $H_0$. A complete orthonormal basis is an orthonormal family whose closed linear span is the whole indicated subspace. These are the compact SVD conventions; in particular, this model concerns minimum-norm representatives in $N(K)^\perp$ and does not estimate a kernel component.

For a truth $x\in N(K)^\perp$, let $\theta_j=\langle x,v_j\rangle_X$. The complete-basis coefficient map identifies $N(K)^\perp$ bijectively and isometrically with $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$, so every $\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ is a model parameter. For $\epsilon>0$, take the functional white-noise experiment on the separable Hilbert space $H_0$ with observations $Y_x(g)=\langle Kx,g\rangle_Y+\epsilon W(g)$, where $W$ is centered, has covariance $\mathbb E[W(g)W(h)]=\langle g,h\rangle_Y$, and has independent standard-normal values on every finite orthonormal tuple. The countable complete basis makes $H_0$ separable. Define $\xi_j=W(u_j)$ and $Z_j=Y_x(u_j)/s_j$. The sequence sample space is $\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$ with the product Borel sigma-algebra, meaning the sigma-algebra generated by its coordinate projections. The coordinate law is the pushforward of the functional experiment under $y\mapsto(y(u_j)/s_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$; this map is measurable because each coordinate is a cylinder evaluation followed by scalar multiplication. The compact SVD expansion gives $\langle Kx,u_j\rangle_Y=s_j\theta_j$, and the positive-noise white-noise coordinate theorem gives the independent standard-normal coordinates $\xi_j$. Hence the normalized coordinates satisfy $Z_j=\theta_j+\epsilon s_j^{-1}\xi_j,\qquad j\in\mathbb N.$

For the zero-noise boundary $\epsilon=0$, define the sequence experiment separately by the point mass at $\theta$, so $Z_j=\theta_j$. This boundary is not an instance of the positive-noise functional experiment.

Let $Q\in[0,\infty)$ and let $a=(a_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$ be a nondecreasing sequence of positive real numbers, so $0<a_1\le a_2\le\cdots$. The statistical ellipsoid of radius $Q$ and weights $a$ in the Gaussian sequence inverse model is
$$\Theta_a(Q)=\left\{\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R):\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}a_j^2\theta_j^2\le Q^2\right\}.$$
No assumption that $a_j\to\infty$ is included. In particular, this definition does not assert that the ellipsoid is compact in $\ell^2$.

Input a normalized sequence observation $z=(z_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}\in\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$ from the Gaussian sequence inverse model and a cutoff $D\in\mathbb N_0$, where $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$. Output the finite-support estimate $\widehat\theta_D(z)\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ defined by
$$\widehat\theta_{D,j}(z)=\begin{cases}z_j,&1\le j\le D,\\0,&j>D.\end{cases}$$
For $D=0$ the output is the zero sequence.

Assume Countable Choice and let $\epsilon\ge0$. In the Gaussian sequence inverse model with positive singular numbers $(s_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$, let $Q\ge0$ and let $(a_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$ be positive and nondecreasing. For each $\theta\in\Theta_a(Q)$, define the squared sequence risk of the cutoff estimator at $D\in\mathbb N_0$ by
$$R_\theta(D):=\mathbb E_\theta\!\left[\|\widehat\theta_D(Z)-\theta\|_{\ell^2}^2\right].$$
Then its exact worst-case squared sequence risk is
$$\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_a(Q)}R_\theta(D)=\frac{Q^2}{a_{D+1}^2}+\epsilon^2\sum_{j=1}^{D}s_j^{-2},$$
where the sum is $0$ for $D=0$. The supremum is attained by the one-coordinate truth $\theta^\star=(Q/a_{D+1})e_{D+1}$, with $\theta^\star=0$ when $Q=0$.

Let $r\ge0$ and $\tau>0$. In the one-dimensional Gaussian location experiment with parameter $\theta\in[-r,r]$, action space $\mathbb R$, observation density
$$p_{\theta,\tau}(y)=\frac{1}{\tau\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{(y-\theta)^2}{2\tau^2}\right)$$
with respect to Lebesgue measure, and squared-error loss, let $M(r,\tau)$ be the minimax expected risk over all measurable deterministic or randomized estimators. Put $b=\min\{r,\tau\}$ and take the prior assigning mass $1/2$ to each of $-b$ and $b$. The better of the estimators $y\mapsto0$ and $y\mapsto y$ has worst-case risk $T(r,\tau)=\min\{r^2,\tau^2\}$, and this prior has Bayes risk at least $T(r,\tau)/\sqrt{2e}$, so $M(r,\tau)\ge T(r,\tau)/\sqrt{2e}$.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]), let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a measurable action space, meaning a set with
a specified sigma-algebra ([[def-measurable-space]]), and let
$L:\Theta\times\mathsf D\to[0,+\infty]$ be a loss function whose section
$a\mapsto L(\theta,a)$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable for each $\theta$. A
randomized decision rule is a probability kernel $\delta$ from the data space
to the action space ([[def-randomized-procedure-as-a-markov-kernel]]). Its
**risk** at $\theta$ is the extended nonnegative number
$$R(\theta,\delta)=\int_{\mathcal X}\left(\int_{\mathsf D}L(\theta,a)\,\delta(x,da)\right)P_\theta(dx).$$
The inner integral is a measurable function of $x$, by
[[lem-procedure-action-law-is-measurable]], so the outer nonnegative integral
is defined by [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]].
A deterministic measurable rule is included by taking its point-mass action
kernel. No measurability on $\Theta$ is required for this definition.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]) and let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a measurable **action space**: a set of available
actions equipped with a sigma-algebra of action events, hence a measurable
space ([[def-measurable-space]]). A **randomized procedure** (or
randomized decision rule) is a probability kernel $K$ from
$(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ to $(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$, in the pointwise sense
of [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. Thus $K(x,\cdot)$ is a
probability measure on $(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ for every $x\in\mathcal X$,
and $x\mapsto K(x,B)$ is $\mathcal A$-measurable for every $B\in\mathcal G$.
After observing $x$, the procedure assigns probability $K(x,B)$ to taking an
action in $B$. The kernel is specified without reference to the unknown
parameter. This definition imposes no measurable structure on $\Theta$. The
kernel is the specification of the procedure; no representation by a separate
random seed is asserted for arbitrary measurable action spaces.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be measurable
parameter and data spaces, with $\Theta$ nonempty, and let
$K:\Theta\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]$ be a probability kernel, writing
$P_\theta=K(\theta,\cdot)$ for the sampling law
([[def-parameter-measurable-statistical-model-as-markov-kernel]]). Let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a nonempty measurable action space
([[def-measurable-space]]). Let $L:\Theta\times\mathsf D\to\overline{\mathbb R}$
be measurable from the product measurable space with sigma-algebra
$\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal G$ to the extended real line with its Borel
sigma-algebra, and assume $L(\theta,a)\geq0$ for all $(\theta,a)$
([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]],
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]], [[def-extended-reals]],
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra-on-the-extended-real-line]]). A **prior** $\pi$ is a
probability measure on $\Theta$. The risk function $\theta\mapsto R(\theta,\delta)$ is measurable
under these hypotheses by kernel integration
([[def-parameter-measurable-statistical-model-as-markov-kernel]],
[[thm-measurability-of-integration-against-a-kernel]]). The **Bayes risk** of
$\delta$ under $\pi$ is
$$r_\pi(\delta)=\int_\Theta R(\theta,\delta)\,\pi(d\theta)\in[0,+\infty].$$
Its **worst-case risk** is
$$R^*(\delta)=\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}R(\theta,\delta)\in[0,+\infty],$$
and the **minimax value** is
$$V_{\rm mm}=\inf\{R^*(\delta):\delta\text{ is a measurable randomized rule from data to actions}\}\in[0,+\infty].$$
These suprema and infima are taken in the extended order on $\overline{\mathbb R}$
([[def-extended-reals]]); they exist by
[[lem-extended-reals-complete]]. The parameter set is nonempty and the rule
class is nonempty under the action-space hypothesis, so these are suprema and
infima of nonempty sets of nonnegative extended risks.
A rule is minimax if its worst-case risk equals this infimum. These definitions
make no assertion that a minimizer exists. Nonemptiness of $\mathsf D$ ensures
the rule class is nonempty: fixing any $a_0\in\mathsf D$ gives the constant
point-mass rule $x\mapsto\delta_{a_0}$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

**The factorial.** By the recursion theorem ([[thm-recursion]]) applied to the
set $\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$, the starting element $(0,1)$ and the function
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot \sigma(k))$, and by the same induction on the
first coordinate as in [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], there is a unique
$F : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with

$$F(0) = 1, \qquad F(\sigma(n)) = F(n)\cdot\sigma(n) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

We write $n! := F(n)$. Thus $0! = 1$, $1! = 0!\cdot 1 = 1$, $2! = 1!\cdot 2 = 2$,
$3! = 6$, $4! = 24$, $5! = 120$, $6! = 720$.

**$0! = 1$ is the base clause of this recursion**, not a convention imported from
elsewhere. Nothing about empty products is presupposed; the agreement with the
empty product is proved below, in clause (a), rather than assumed.

**Truncated difference.** Throughout, $n - k$ is the operation fixed in
[[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]]: the unique $j$ with $k + j = n$ when
$k \le n$, and $0$ when $n < k$.

**The falling factorial.** For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ define $n^{\underline{k}}$ by
recursion on $k$, by the recursion theorem applied to
$\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$ with starting element $(0,1)$ and
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot (n-k))$:

$$n^{\underline{0}} = 1, \qquad n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k) .$$

So $n^{\underline{1}} = 1\cdot(n-0) = n$ and $n^{\underline{2}} = n\,(n-1)$, and
for $k \le n$ the value is the product $n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)$ of the $k$ topmost
factors.

**Four facts, proved here because the page uses each of them.**

**(a) The factorial is the product of the first $n$ positive naturals.**
$n! = \prod_{j<n}\sigma(j) = \prod_{j<n}(j+1)$, the $\mathbb{N}$-valued product of
[[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]]. Induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]): at
$n = 0$ both sides are $1$, the empty product and the base clause agreeing; and
$\prod_{j<\sigma(n)}\sigma(j) = \big(\prod_{j<n}\sigma(j)\big)\cdot\sigma(n) = n!\cdot\sigma(n) = \sigma(n)!$.
**So the empty-product reading and the base-clause reading are the same reading**,
and neither was assumed.

**(b) $n! \ne 0$, and $\iota(n!) = \prod^{\mathbb{R}}_{j<n}\iota(j+1)$.** For the
first, $0! = 1 \ne 0$ ([[thm-omega-is-peano-system]]) and
$\sigma(n)! = n!\cdot\sigma(n)$ is a product of two nonzero naturals, which is
nonzero: if $xy = 0$ with $y \ne 0$ then $xy = 0\cdot y$
([[lem-nat-mult-identity]]) and cancellation gives $x = 0$
([[lem-nat-mult-cancellative]]). So $n! \ne 0$ for every $n$ by induction. For the second, apply the bridge clause
6 of that lemma to clause (a) above. This is what makes the factorial of this
page and the real-valued product $\prod_{j<n}(j+1)$ used elsewhere in the library
**one object seen twice**, rather than two unrelated notions.

**(c) $n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$ for $k \le n$.** Induction on $k$, for
all $n$ at once. At $k = 0$ this reads $1 \cdot n! = n!$. Assume it at $k$ and
let $\sigma(k) \le n$; then $k \le n$, and writing $d := n - k$ we have
$k + d = n$ and $d \ne 0$, since $k + 0 = k \ne n$; so $d = \sigma(e)$ for a
unique $e$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]), and $\sigma(k) + e = n$, that is
$e = n - \sigma(k)$ ([[lem-nat-add-cancellative]]). Therefore
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}}\cdot\big(n-\sigma(k)\big)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)\cdot e! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\big(e!\cdot\sigma(e)\big) = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\sigma(e)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$,
using commutativity and associativity of multiplication
([[lem-nat-mult-associative]], [[lem-nat-mult-commutative]]) and the recursion
clause for the factorial.

**(d) Boundary values.** $n^{\underline{0}} = 1$ for every $n$, by the base
clause; $n^{\underline{n}} = n!$, since clause (c) at $k = n$ gives
$n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0! = n!$ and $0! = 1$; and
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ whenever $k > n$. For the last, $n - n = 0$ gives
$n^{\underline{\sigma(n)}} = n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0 = 0$, the clause
$x \cdot 0 = 0$ being definitional ([[def-nat-multiplication]]), and if
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ then
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = 0$ as well, so $n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ for every
$k \ge \sigma(n)$ by induction.

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges ([[def-series]]) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ and let $\mathcal A=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. If finite measures $\mu$ and $
u$ on $(X,\mathcal A)$ agree on $\mathcal P$ and satisfy $\mu(X)=
u(X)$, then $\mu=
u$ on $\mathcal A$.

The total-mass equality is separate because this library's pi-system convention does not require $X\in\mathcal P$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty. The following are equivalent.

1. $A$ is compact.
2. $A$ is closed and bounded.
3. $A$ is pseudocompact.
4. Every continuous $f:A\to\mathbb{R}$ attains a maximum and a minimum on $A$.

This theorem is a ZF statement. The nonemptiness hypothesis is necessary for condition 4, because the empty image has neither a maximum nor a minimum.

If $f:X\to Y$ is continuous between topological spaces, then
$f^{-1}[B]\in\mathcal B(X)$ for every $B\in\mathcal B(Y)$.

derivations.claim: If $Q=0$, then $\Theta_a(Q)=\{0\}$. The zero estimator has minimax risk zero, and the $D=0$ cutoff expression is also zero, so the asserted inequalities hold. Hence assume $Q>0$.

Put $\tau_j^2=\epsilon^2s_j^{-2}$ and let $\mathcal C$ be the set of sequences $r_j\ge0$ with $\sum_j a_j^2r_j\le Q^2$. For $r\in\mathcal C$, define $J(r)=\sum_j\min(r_j,\tau_j^2)$. Since $a_j\ge a_1>0$, one has $\sum_jr_j\le Q^2/a_1^2$, so $J(r)$ is finite.

As $s_j\to0$ and $\epsilon>0$, $\tau_j^2\to\infty$. Choose $N\ge1$ so that $\tau_j^2>Q^2/a_1^2$ for $j>N$. Every feasible $r$ then has $r_j<\tau_j^2$ on that tail. Replacing its tail by $\widetilde r_{N+1}=(\sum_{j>N}a_j^2r_j)/a_{N+1}^2$ at coordinate $N+1$ and zero thereafter preserves the weighted budget and does not decrease $J$, because $a_j\ge a_{N+1}$ for $j>N$ and $\sum_{j>N}r_j\le\widetilde r_{N+1}<\tau_{N+1}^2$. The finite-dimensional feasible set in coordinates $1,\ldots,N+1$ is nonempty (it contains zero), closed, and bounded (each coordinate is at most $Q^2/a_j^2$). The finite sum $J$ is continuous there, so [F9] gives a finite-support maximizer $r^*$.

From [F7], for $n\ge3$ one has $n!\ge6\cdot3^{n-3}$, with strict inequality for some $n$, so $e=1+1+\frac12+\sum_{n\ge3}1/n!<2+\frac12+\frac16\sum_{k\ge0}3^{-k}=\frac{11}{4}$. Hence $2\sqrt{2e}<\sqrt{22}<\frac{121}{25}=(\frac{11}{5})^2$.

The compact-SVD coordinate realization uses Countable Choice [A1]. statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $X$ and $Y$ be real Hilbert spaces and let $K:X\to Y$ be a compact linear operator of infinite rank, viewed as an inverse model with exact datum $Kx$. Here compact means that the image of every bounded subset has compact closure. Write $N(K)=\{x\in X:Kx=0\}$ and $H_0=\overline{\operatorname{ran}K}$. Fix a positive singular system $(s_j,v_j,u_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$ for $K$, where $\mathbb N=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$, $s_1\ge s_2\ge\cdots>0$, $s_j\to0$, $Kv_j=s_ju_j$, $(v_j)$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $N(K)^\perp$, and $(u_j)$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $H_0$. A complete orthonormal basis is an orthonormal family whose closed linear span is the whole indicated subspace. These are the compact SVD conventions; in particular, this model concerns minimum-norm representatives in $N(K)^\perp$ and does not estimate a kernel component.

For a truth $x\in N(K)^\perp$, let $\theta_j=\langle x,v_j\rangle_X$. The complete-basis coefficient map identifies $N(K)^\perp$ bijectively and isometrically with $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$, so every $\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ is a model parameter. For $\epsilon>0$, take the functional white-noise experiment on the separable Hilbert space $H_0$ with observations $Y_x(g)=\langle Kx,g\rangle_Y+\epsilon W(g)$, where $W$ is centered, has covariance $\mathbb E[W(g)W(h)]=\langle g,h\rangle_Y$, and has independent standard-normal values on every finite orthonormal tuple. The countable complete basis makes $H_0$ separable. Define $\xi_j=W(u_j)$ and $Z_j=Y_x(u_j)/s_j$. The sequence sample space is $\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$ with the product Borel sigma-algebra, meaning the sigma-algebra generated by its coordinate projections. The coordinate law is the pushforward of the functional experiment under $y\mapsto(y(u_j)/s_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$; this map is measurable because each coordinate is a cylinder evaluation followed by scalar multiplication. The compact SVD expansion gives $\langle Kx,u_j\rangle_Y=s_j\theta_j$, and the positive-noise white-noise coordinate theorem gives the independent standard-normal coordinates $\xi_j$. Hence the normalized coordinates satisfy $Z_j=\theta_j+\epsilon s_j^{-1}\xi_j,\qquad j\in\mathbb N.$

For the zero-noise boundary $\epsilon=0$, define the sequence experiment separately by the point mass at $\theta$, so $Z_j=\theta_j$. This boundary is not an instance of the positive-noise functional experiment.

Let $Q\in[0,\infty)$ and let $a=(a_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$ be a nondecreasing sequence of positive real numbers, so $0<a_1\le a_2\le\cdots$. The statistical ellipsoid of radius $Q$ and weights $a$ in the Gaussian sequence inverse model is
$$\Theta_a(Q)=\left\{\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R):\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}a_j^2\theta_j^2\le Q^2\right\}.$$
No assumption that $a_j\to\infty$ is included. In particular, this definition does not assert that the ellipsoid is compact in $\ell^2$.

In the Gaussian sequence inverse model with positive singular numbers $(s_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$, let $Q\ge0$ and let $(a_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$ be positive and nondecreasing. For each $\theta\in\Theta_a(Q)$, define the squared sequence risk of the cutoff estimator at $D\in\mathbb N_0$ by
$$R_\theta(D):=\mathbb E_\theta\!\left[\|\widehat\theta_D(Z)-\theta\|_{\ell^2}^2\right].$$
Then its exact worst-case squared sequence risk is
$$\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_a(Q)}R_\theta(D)=\frac{Q^2}{a_{D+1}^2}+\epsilon^2\sum_{j=1}^{D}s_j^{-2},$$
where the sum is $0$ for $D=0$. The supremum is attained by the one-coordinate truth $\theta^\star=(Q/a_{D+1})e_{D+1}$, with $\theta^\star=0$ when $Q=0$.

$$\Theta_a(Q)=\left\{\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R):\sum_{j\ge1}a_j^2\theta_j^2\le Q^2\right\}.$$
Let $R_*(\epsilon)$ be the square root of the minimax expected squared $\ell^2$ error over all measurable deterministic or randomized estimators from the product Borel data space to $\ell^2$, and put
$$R_{\rm cut}(\epsilon)=\left[\inf_{D\in\mathbb N_0}\left\{\frac{Q^2}{a_{D+1}^2}+\epsilon^2\sum_{j=1}^{D}s_j^{-2}\right\}\right]^{1/2},\qquad\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}.$$

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For $a>0$ and $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$a^x:=\exp(x\log a).$$
For the supplementary zero-base convention, define $0^x:=0$ when $x>0$.

The expressions $0^0$ and $0^x$ for $x<0$ are left undefined. Negative bases are not assigned arbitrary real powers.

For $a,b>0$ and $r,s\in\mathbb R$,
$$a^{r+s}=a^ra^s,\qquad (ab)^r=a^rb^r,\qquad (a/b)^r=a^r/b^r,\qquad (a^r)^s=a^{rs}.$$

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and
$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges ([[def-series]]) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

Suppose $s_j\asymp e^{-pj}$ and $a_j\asymp e^{\kappa j}$. Let $L=\log(1/\epsilon)$ and $D_0=\lfloor L/(p+\kappa)\rfloor$.
